# Abstract

Published regression equations for estimating stature from tibial length differ between populations, but whether this reflects genuine population differences or sampling variation around a common coefficient is unresolved. We conducted a systematic review and random-effects meta-regression of studies reporting simple linear regression of stature on percutaneous tibial length in adults. Three databases were searched in April 2026, and risk of bias was assessed with an adapted Prediction model Risk Of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST). The primary analysis excluded models at high risk of bias in the analysis domain; the full sample was analysed for sensitivity. Fifty-four studies contributed `r o$rob_n` equations, of which `r o$allstudies_k` entered the meta-regression. The primary pooled coefficient was `r f3(o$primary_b)` cm of stature per cm of tibial length (95% CI `r ci(o$primary_lb, o$primary_ub)`; k = `r o$primary_k`), with very high heterogeneity (I² = `r f1(o$primary_I2)`%). Country was a significant moderator (p `r fp(o$country_primary_p)`), explaining `r f0(o$country_primary_R2)`% of between-study variance; continental grouping was not (p `r fp(o$continent_primary_p)`). Male and female coefficients did not differ (`r f3(o$primary_male_b)` vs `r f3(o$primary_female_b)`; p `r fp(o$primary_sex_p)`). Estimates were stable in sensitivity analyses (full sample `r f3(o$allstudies_b)`; low risk of bias only `r f3(o$lowOnly_b)`; samples aged 18 years and over only `r f3(o$age18_b)`). Funnel-plot asymmetry was attributable to four high-leverage equations. Equations further from the pooled coefficient reported larger standard errors of the estimate (r = `r f3(o$offset_r)`, p `r fp(o$offset_p)`). The tibia–stature coefficient is best described as a robust global central tendency with modest country-level variation; combined with a population-specific intercept, it offers a practical default where validated local equations are unavailable.

**Keywords:** Stature estimation; Tibia; Forensic anthropology; Anthropometry; Meta-regression; Systematic review

# Introduction

Accurate estimation of stature from skeletal or partial remains is a core task of forensic anthropology. It contributes directly to the biological profile used to narrow the pool of possible identities in cases involving unidentified, fragmented or commingled human remains, and plays a comparable role in bioarchaeological reconstruction of past populations. Because complete skeletons are frequently unavailable, stature is most often inferred from the length of one or more long bones using a regression equation of the form stature = a + b × (bone length), where a is the intercept and b is the regression coefficient (slope) relating a unit change in bone length to the corresponding change in stature.

The modern foundation for this approach was laid by Trotter and Gleser [@trotter1952; @trotter1958], whose equations, derived from American soldiers who died during the Second World War and the Korean War, remain among the most widely cited stature-estimation formulae in forensic practice. These equations, and most of those published since, were developed separately for named population or ancestry groups and for each sex, reflecting a long-standing assumption that the relationship between long-bone length and stature is population-specific, so that a formula developed in one group cannot safely be applied to another. This assumption has been reinforced by studies documenting secular changes in body proportions and differences in limb-to-trunk proportions across ancestry groups, and by demonstrations that applying an equation derived in one population to another can bias stature estimates by several centimetres.

A parallel line of research has questioned whether population-specific equations are necessary. Feldesman and colleagues [@feldesman1990] evaluated the femur/stature ratio across 51 population samples totalling roughly 13,000 individuals and reported a mean ratio of 26.74% with a very restricted range of variation and no significant sex difference; a subsequent study using bootstrap resampling [@feldesman1996] found that apparent racial differences in this ratio did not hold up as a practically meaningful source of error once sampling variability was accounted for. Sjøvold [@sjovold1990] proposed the weighted line of organic correlation, fitted across a wide range of population samples, and concluded that the effects of sex and race on this line were practically negligible. More recently, Albanese and colleagues [@albanese2016] developed univariate and multivariate equations for the major long bones, including the tibia, explicitly as an alternative to population- and group-specific formulae; a validation study in a South African sample [@bidmos2024] found that these generic equations produce usable, though not always unbiased, estimates, and concluded that population-specific equations remain preferable where population affiliation can be confidently assigned.

Despite this body of work, the debate has been conducted largely through primary data collection within single studies or skeletal collections, or through simple averaging of ratios or coefficients, rather than through formal quantitative synthesis of the published literature with the methods now standard in evidence-based medicine: random-effects meta-analysis with explicit quantification of between-study heterogeneity, formal testing of candidate moderators such as ethnicity or geography, and assessment of small-study effects and publication bias. Among the long bones, the tibia is of particular practical interest: it is the second-longest bone in the body, is easily measured percutaneously in living subjects as well as in skeletal remains, and has repeatedly been reported to correlate more strongly with stature than the upper-limb long bones. To our knowledge, no previous study has used formal random-effects meta-regression to test whether the tibia–stature regression coefficient behaves as a global constant, in the sense of showing no ethnic or geographic moderation beyond sampling error, or whether it varies systematically with population.

This study addresses that gap through a systematic review and meta-regression of published studies reporting simple linear regression equations for predicting stature from percutaneous tibial length in adults. The central hypothesis is that the variation observed in the published regression coefficient (b) can be explained by random sampling variation rather than by systematic ethnic or racial differences; in other words, that the coefficient behaves as a global constant. The hypothesis was tested with random-effects meta-regression, with country and continental grouping as categorical moderators, alongside secondary analyses of sex, risk of bias, publication bias, and the relationship between each study's deviation from the pooled coefficient and its own reported goodness of fit.

# Materials and methods

The review is reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement [@page2021]. The review protocol was not registered and no separate protocol document was prepared.

## Eligibility criteria

Eligible studies were conducted in living adults and developed a simple linear regression equation predicting stature from percutaneous tibial length, reporting the unstandardized regression coefficient or the data needed to compute it. Tibial length was defined as the distance from the medial condyle (or medial knee joint line) of the tibia to the tip of the medial malleolus, measured over the skin. Studies were excluded if tibial length was measured radiologically or on cadavers or dry bone, if only multivariable equations were reported, if a different landmark set was used (for example, lateral condyle to lateral malleolus, or tibial tuberosity to medial malleolus), or if the sample included children. Adult samples were defined as samples recruited from age 18 years or above; samples of young adults whose lower age bound was 17 years were accepted, and their influence was examined in a sensitivity analysis. Only reports published in English were eligible.

Sex-specific equations from the same study were entered as separate effect sizes. Where a study reported both sex-specific equations and a combined-sex equation derived from the same participants, only the sex-specific equations were pooled, to avoid counting participants twice. Where several reports drew on overlapping samples, the reports with non-overlapping samples were retained and the overlapping report was excluded from the quantitative synthesis.

## Information sources and search strategy

Google Scholar, PubMed and Scopus were searched between 10 and 15 April 2026 using the terms "stature", "stature estimation", "tibia" and "tibial length", combined as "stature estimation" AND ("tibia" OR "tibial length"). The same search string was used in all three databases, with no date, language or other database filters; the restriction to English-language reports was applied as an eligibility criterion during screening. The number of records retrieved from each source is shown in Fig. 1.

## Study selection

Titles and abstracts were screened independently by two reviewers against the eligibility criteria, followed by independent full-text screening by the same reviewers. Full texts were sought from publishers, open-access repositories and indexing services; reports whose full text could not be obtained were recorded as not retrieved. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or, where necessary, by referral to a third reviewer.

## Data extraction

Data were extracted independently by two reviewers using a piloted form adapted from the CHARMS checklist [@moons2014] for single-predictor equations. For each eligible equation, the following were extracted: first author and year; country and population or ethnic group; setting and sampling method; sample size; sex; age range; the landmarks, technique and instrument used to measure tibial length; the method used to measure stature; the intercept and unstandardized regression coefficient (b) with its standard error or 95% confidence interval; the correlation coefficient (r) or coefficient of determination (R²); and the standard error of the estimate (SEE), where reported. Any validation of the equation reported by the authors was also recorded and classified according to TRIPOD definitions as external (performance assessed in independent data from a different setting, time or population), internal (a split sample or holdout from the derivation data) or none; agreement between predicted and observed stature within the derivation sample itself was treated as apparent performance rather than validation. Sex was recorded as the binary male or female classification reported by the source studies; gender was not reported and could not be analysed.

Where the standard error of b, SE(b), was not reported it was derived in the following order of priority: (1) SE(b) = SEE / (SD~x~ × √(N − 1)), where SD~x~ is the standard deviation of tibial length; (2) SE(b) = [SD~y~ × √(1 − r²)] / [SD~x~ × √(N − 2)], where SD~y~ is the standard deviation of stature; (3) SE(b) = b / t, from the reported t-statistic or p-value; and (4) back-calculation from the 95% confidence interval. Equations for which SE(b) could not be obtained were described but not pooled. Reported statistics were cross-checked for internal consistency (for example, agreement between reported SEE, R² and standard deviations), and implausible values were checked against the source; a units error found in this way (an SEE recorded in millimetres) was corrected before analysis.

## Risk of bias and applicability

Risk of bias was assessed independently by two reviewers using an adaptation of the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool (PROBAST) [@wolff2019]. Signalling questions concerning the selection of and adjustment for multiple candidate predictors were marked not applicable. Four domains were rated low, high or unclear risk of bias: participants, predictor (measurement of tibial length), outcome (measurement of stature) and analysis. The analysis domain included checks of the internal consistency of each study's reported regression statistics. Overall risk of bias was rated high if any domain was high, unclear if any domain was unclear and none high, and low otherwise. Applicability concerns were rated for the participants, predictor and outcome domains. Disagreements were resolved by consensus.

## Statistical analysis

All analyses were performed in R using the metafor package [@metafor]. The regression coefficient b was the effect size and its sampling variance was SE(b)². Pooled estimates were obtained from random-effects models fitted by restricted maximum likelihood (REML). Because the analysis-domain rating reflects the internal trustworthiness of each reported coefficient, the primary analysis excluded models at high risk of bias in this domain; the full sample was analysed as a sensitivity analysis.

To test the study hypothesis, country (as the available proxy for population or ethnic group) was entered as a categorical moderator in a random-effects meta-regression, and continental grouping was examined in the same way as a robustness check. Moderator significance was assessed with the omnibus QM test and the proportion of between-study variance explained was expressed as an R² analogue. A non-significant QM test was interpreted as consistent with a global coefficient. Heterogeneity was quantified with Cochran's Q, I² and τ² [@higgins2002]. Sex was analysed as a moderator and sex-specific pooled coefficients were estimated.

Sensitivity analyses comprised the full sample, restriction to models at low risk of bias, exclusion of samples with a lower age bound of 17 years, a meta-regression with risk-of-bias category as moderator, and leave-one-out analysis. Small-study effects were assessed with funnel plots and Egger's regression test [@egger1997], and the trim-and-fill method [@duval2000] was used to estimate the number of potentially missing studies. Where asymmetry was detected, the influence of the studies driving it was examined by refitting the model without them.

As a secondary analysis, the absolute difference between each model's coefficient and the primary pooled coefficient (offset = |b~i~ − b~pooled~|) was correlated with that model's reported SEE, using Pearson and Spearman correlation and unweighted and inverse-variance-weighted regression. This analysis used all models with an available SEE, including those at high risk of bias, and was repeated within risk-of-bias strata. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.

# Results

## Study selection

The searches identified `r fmt(pv["google"] + pv["pubmed"] + pv["scopus"])` records (Google Scholar `r fmt(pv["google"])`, PubMed `r fmt(pv["pubmed"])`, Scopus `r fmt(pv["scopus"])`). After removal of `r fmt(pv["google"] + pv["pubmed"] + pv["scopus"] - pv["after_dedup"])` duplicates, `r fmt(pv["after_dedup"])` records were screened by title and abstract and `r fmt(pv["after_title_abstract"])` full-text reports were sought. Of these, `r pv["not_retrieved"]` could not be retrieved and `r pv["after_title_abstract"] - pv["not_retrieved"]` were assessed for eligibility, of which `r pv["after_title_abstract"] - pv["not_retrieved"] - pv["after_fulltext"]` were excluded (Supplementary Table S2). Fifty-four studies were included `r cite_all`, contributing `r o$rob_n` sex-specific simple linear regression equations (Fig. 1). Four equations were not pooled: one (female equation of Mundane et al. [@mundane2023]) because SE(b) could not be derived; one combined-sex equation (Gualdi-Russo et al. [@gualdirusso2018]) because it re-used the participants of that study's male and female equations; and two equations from a national survey of Kosovan school-leavers [@gardasevic2019] because the survey overlapped the regional samples reported separately [@gardasevic2018; @arifi2021]. The meta-regression therefore included `r o$allstudies_k` equations from `r pv["studies_in_synthesis"]` studies.

```{r fig1, fig.cap = "Fig. 1. PRISMA 2020 flow diagram of study selection.", out.width = "90%"}
knitr::include_graphics("Figure1_PRISMA_flow_diagram.png")
```

## Risk of bias and applicability

Risk of bias was low for most of the `r o$rob_n` extracted equations in the participant (`r o$rob_D1_RoB_Low` of `r o$rob_n`), predictor (`r o$rob_D2_RoB_Low`) and outcome (`r o$rob_D3_RoB_Low`) domains, with the remainder rated unclear; no equation was rated high risk of bias in these domains (Fig. 2). Risk of bias in the analysis domain was more variable: `r o$rob_D4_RoB_Low` equations (`r pct(o$rob_D4_RoB_Low, o$rob_n)`) were rated low, `r o$rob_D4_RoB_High` (`r pct(o$rob_D4_RoB_High, o$rob_n)`) high and `r o$rob_D4_RoB_Unclear` (`r pct(o$rob_D4_RoB_Unclear, o$rob_n)`) unclear. High ratings most often reflected internally inconsistent reporting, such as a stated SEE that could not be reconciled with the study's own R² and standard deviations, rather than deficiencies in design or measurement. Applicability concerns were low for most equations with respect to participants (`r o$rob_D1_App_Low` of `r o$rob_n`), with `r o$rob_D1_App_High` rated high concern, principally because of age ranges extending well beyond young and middle adulthood, and `r o$rob_D1_App_Unclear` unclear.

`r if (o$val_external == 0) "None" else o$val_external` of the `r o$rob_n` equations had been externally validated. `r tools::toTitleCase(num_words[o$val_internal + 1])` equations from `r num_words[o$val_internal_studies + 1]` studies were internally validated on a split sample or holdout drawn from the derivation data [@duyar2003; @gualdirusso2018; @sacoledo2019; @sacoledo2020; @banyeh2022]. A further `r o$val_other` equations from `r num_words[o$val_other_studies + 1]` studies reported checks that do not constitute validation (agreement between predicted and observed stature in the derivation sample, comparison with published equations in the same sample, comparison of coefficients between two samples, or measurement reliability only), and the remaining `r o$val_none` (`r pct(o$val_none, o$rob_n)`) reported no validation of any kind.

Of the `r o$allstudies_k` equations eligible for pooling, `r n_high_pooled` were at high risk of bias in the analysis domain and were excluded from the primary analysis, leaving `r o$primary_k` equations (`r o$primary_k - n_unclear_primary` low and `r n_unclear_primary` unclear risk of bias) from `r pv["studies_in_primary"]` studies.

```{r fig2, fig.cap = sprintf("Fig. 2. Summary of (a) risk of bias and (b) applicability concerns by PROBAST domain and overall, across the %d extracted equations. A per-equation plot is given in Supplementary Fig. S1.", o$rob_n), out.width = "85%"}
knitr::include_graphics("Figure2_RoB_Applicability_Summary.png")
```

## Characteristics of the included equations

The primary dataset comprised `r o$primary_k` equations from `r o$primary_countries` countries: `r o$primary_country_counts`. Sample sizes ranged from `r o$primary_N_min` to `r o$primary_N_max` participants per equation (median `r o$primary_N_median`; total `r fmt(o$primary_N_total)`), and publication years from `r o$primary_year_min` to `r o$primary_year_max`. There were `r o$primary_male_k` male and `r o$primary_female_k` female equations. The full dataset (k = `r o$allstudies_k`) drew on `r o$full_countries` countries in `r o$full_continents` regional groupings (`r o$full_continent_counts`), with a total of `r fmt(o$full_N_total)` participants; Indian studies contributed `r o$full_india` of the `r o$allstudies_k` equations (Fig. 3). Characteristics of every equation are given in Supplementary Table S1.

```{r fig3, fig.cap = sprintf("Fig. 3. Characteristics of the %d equations included in the meta-regression: (A) country, (B) sex, (C) sample size and (D) publication year.", o$allstudies_k), out.width = "100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("Figure3_Study_Characteristics.png")
```

## Pooled coefficient and geographic moderators

In the primary analysis the pooled regression coefficient was `r f3(o$primary_b)` (95% CI `r ci(o$primary_lb, o$primary_ub)`; z = `r f2(o$primary_z)`, p `r fp(o$primary_p)`; Table 1, Fig. 4): on average, each additional centimetre of tibial length was associated with about `r f2(o$primary_b)` cm of additional stature. The full-sample estimate was similar (`r f3(o$allstudies_b)`; 95% CI `r ci(o$allstudies_lb, o$allstudies_ub)`), with overlapping confidence intervals.

Country was a significant moderator in the primary analysis (QM = `r f2(o$country_primary_QM)`, df = `r o$country_primary_df`, p `r fp(o$country_primary_p)`), explaining `r f1(o$country_primary_R2)`% of between-study variance (residual I² = `r f2(o$country_primary_I2res)`%). Relative to the reference category (`r o$country_primary_reference`), only Nigerian studies differed significantly (`r o$country_primary_sig`). In the full sample, country was of borderline significance (QM = `r f2(o$country_full_QM)`, df = `r o$country_full_df`, p `r fp(o$country_full_p)`; R² analogue `r f1(o$country_full_R2)`%). Continental grouping was not a significant moderator in either the primary analysis (QM = `r f2(o$continent_primary_QM)`, df = `r o$continent_primary_df`, p `r fp(o$continent_primary_p)`; R² analogue `r f1(o$continent_primary_R2)`%) or the full sample (p `r fp(o$continent_full_p)`; R² analogue `r f1(o$continent_full_R2)`%).

             caption = "Table 1. Pooled regression coefficient, moderator tests and heterogeneity in the primary analysis and the full-sample sensitivity analysis. For moderator models, I² is residual heterogeneity.")
```

```{r fig4, fig.cap = sprintf("Fig. 4. Forest plot of the regression coefficient (b) for the %d equations in the primary analysis, with the random-effects pooled estimate.", o$primary_k), out.width = "80%"}
knitr::include_graphics("Figure4_Forest_Overall.png")
```

## Heterogeneity

Heterogeneity was very high in the primary analysis (I² = `r f2(o$primary_I2)`%, τ² = `r f3(o$primary_tau2)`; Q(`r o$primary_k - 1`) = `r f2(o$primary_QE)`, p < 0.0001), meaning that less than 3% of the variability in reported coefficients was attributable to sampling error, and was essentially unchanged in the full sample (I² = `r f2(o$allstudies_I2)`%, τ² = `r f3(o$allstudies_tau2)`). Country accounted for a modest share of this heterogeneity, leaving most of it unexplained.

## Sensitivity analyses

Pooled estimates were stable across sensitivity analyses (Table 2). Restricting the sample to equations at low risk of bias (k = `r o$lowOnly_k`) gave `r f3(o$lowOnly_b)` (95% CI `r ci(o$lowOnly_lb, o$lowOnly_ub)`), and excluding the `r n_age17_primary` primary-analysis equations from samples with a lower age bound of 17 years (k = `r o$age18_k`) gave `r f3(o$age18_b)` (95% CI `r ci(o$age18_lb, o$age18_ub)`). Heterogeneity remained above 97% in every subset. Risk-of-bias category was not a significant moderator in the full sample (QM = `r f2(o$robmod_QM)`, df = `r o$robmod_df`, p `r fp(o$robmod_p)`; R² analogue `r f1(o$robmod_R2)`%), although equations at high risk of bias had a lower coefficient on average than those at low risk (difference `r f3(o$robmod_high_est)`, p `r fp(o$robmod_high_p)`). In leave-one-out analysis the primary pooled estimate ranged from `r f3(o$loo_min)` (omitting `r o$loo_min_study`) to `r f3(o$loo_max)` (omitting `r o$loo_max_study`), and I² from `r f2(o$loo_I2_min)`% to `r f2(o$loo_I2_max)`%, so no single equation materially influenced the result.

```{r table2}
knitr::kable(setNames(table2[, 1:7], c("Analysis", "k", "Pooled b", "95% CI", "τ²", "I² (%)", "Q (df)")), format = "simple",
             caption = "Table 2. Pooled regression coefficient and heterogeneity across sensitivity analyses (p < 0.0001 for Q in every analysis).")
```

## Publication bias

The funnel plot for the primary analysis was asymmetric (Fig. 5), with a group of equations with large standard errors and high coefficients on the right, and Egger's test was significant (z = `r f2(o$egger_primary_z)`, p `r fp(o$egger_primary_p)`); the same was true of the full sample (z = `r f2(o$egger_full_z)`, p `r fp(o$egger_full_p)`; Fig. 6). Trim-and-fill imputed no missing studies in either analysis (k~0~ = `r o$tf_primary_k0` and `r o$tf_full_k0`). The asymmetry was driven by four equations with both markedly higher coefficients and larger standard errors than the rest: the male and female equations of Esomonu et al. [@esomonu2016], the male equation of Tiwari and Datta [@tiwari2022] and the female equation of Okwan et al. [@okwan2025], all at low risk of bias. Excluding them (k = `r o$outlier_k`) gave a pooled coefficient of `r f3(o$outlier_b)` (95% CI `r ci(o$outlier_lb, o$outlier_ub)`) and Egger's test was no longer significant (z = `r f2(o$outlier_egger_z)`, p `r fp(o$outlier_egger_p)`). The very steep male coefficient of Tiwari and Datta (4.923) is consistent with that study's own summary statistics; it coincides with an unusually narrow spread of tibial length in that sample (SD 1.00 cm, against 2–3 cm in most studies).

```{r fig56, fig.cap = sprintf("Fig. 5. Funnel plot, primary analysis (k = %d).    Fig. 6. Funnel plot, full-sample sensitivity analysis (k = %d).", o$primary_k, o$allstudies_k), out.width = "49%", fig.show = "hold"}
knitr::include_graphics(c("Figure5_Funnel_Primary.png", "Figure6_Funnel_AllStudies.png"))
```

## Offset from the pooled coefficient and model fit

Across the `r o$offset_k` equations with an available SEE (including `r o$offset_high_n` at high risk of bias), the absolute offset from the primary pooled coefficient (`r f3(o$offset_ref_b)`) was positively correlated with the reported SEE (Pearson r = `r f3(o$offset_r)`, p `r fp(o$offset_p)`; Spearman ρ = `r f3(o$offset_rho)`, p `r fp(o$offset_rho_p)`; Fig. 7). In unweighted regression, each unit of offset was associated with an SEE `r f2(o$offset_slope)` cm higher (SE `r f2(o$offset_slope_se)`, p `r fp(o$offset_slope_p)`, R² = `r f1(100 * o$offset_R2)`%); the inverse-variance-weighted slope was similar but not significant (`r f2(o$offset_wslope)`, SE `r f2(o$offset_wslope_se)`, p `r fp(o$offset_wslope_p)`). The association was stronger among equations at high risk of bias (n = `r o$offset_high_n`; r = `r f3(o$offset_high_r)`, p `r fp(o$offset_high_p)`) than among those at low or unclear risk (n = `r o$offset_low_n`; r = `r f3(o$offset_low_r)`, p `r fp(o$offset_low_p)`), although mean absolute offset was similar in the two groups (`r f3(o$offset_high_mean)` and `r f3(o$offset_low_mean)`).

```{r fig7, fig.cap = sprintf("Fig. 7. Absolute offset from the primary pooled coefficient against reported SEE for %d equations. Triangles: high risk of bias; circles: low or unclear risk of bias. Line: unweighted least-squares fit.", o$offset_k), out.width = "75%"}
knitr::include_graphics("Figure7_OffsetVsSEE.png")
```

## Sex

In the primary analysis the male pooled coefficient was `r f3(o$primary_male_b)` (95% CI `r ci(o$primary_male_lb, o$primary_male_ub)`; k = `r o$primary_male_k`) and the female pooled coefficient `r f3(o$primary_female_b)` (95% CI `r ci(o$primary_female_lb, o$primary_female_ub)`; k = `r o$primary_female_k`), with no significant difference (QM = `r f3(o$primary_sex_QM)`, df = 1, p `r fp(o$primary_sex_p)`; Fig. 8). The full sample gave the same pattern (males `r f3(o$full_male_b)`, 95% CI `r ci(o$full_male_lb, o$full_male_ub)`, k = `r o$full_male_k`; females `r f3(o$full_female_b)`, 95% CI `r ci(o$full_female_lb, o$full_female_ub)`, k = `r o$full_female_k`; p `r fp(o$full_sex_p)`).

```{r fig8, fig.cap = "Fig. 8. Forest plots of the regression coefficient by sex, primary analysis: (A) male and (B) female equations.", out.width = "100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("Figure8_Forest_BySex.png")

# Discussion

This review tested whether the coefficient linking percutaneous tibial length to stature behaves as a global constant. The primary analysis yielded a pooled coefficient of `r f3(o$primary_b)` (95% CI `r ci(o$primary_lb, o$primary_ub)`), a precisely estimated central tendency. At the same time, country was a significant moderator and heterogeneity remained very high (I² = `r f1(o$primary_I2)`%) after accounting for it. The evidence is therefore neither a clean confirmation nor a clean rejection of the hypothesis: there is a robust central tendency in the tibia–stature relationship, but it coexists with detectable country-level structure that a strict global-constant model would not predict.

The contrast between the country-level effect and the non-significant continental effect is informative. If population differences in the coefficient reflected broad continental ancestry, the continental moderator should have performed at least as well as the more granular country moderator; instead, country explained more variance than continent in both analyses. Whatever systematic variation exists is therefore more plausibly attributable to national- or population-level factors, which may include genuine differences in body proportions but may equally reflect methodological practices that cluster by country or research group, such as consistent choices of landmark, instrument or recruitment strategy, than to broad racial categories. The country effect was also less robust than the pooled coefficient itself: it was of borderline significance in the full sample (p `r fp(o$country_full_p)`) and rested largely on the Nigerian studies.

Restricting the analysis to studies with internally consistent reporting did not reduce heterogeneity: I² was `r f1(o$allstudies_I2)`% in the full sample, `r f1(o$primary_I2)`% in the primary analysis and `r f1(o$lowOnly_I2)`% among low-risk-of-bias equations, and risk-of-bias category explained only `r f1(o$robmod_R2)`% of variance. The very high heterogeneity is therefore not mainly an artefact of weaker studies, and more plausibly reflects genuine variation across populations compounded by methodological differences not captured by the risk-of-bias domains. Excluding high-risk-of-bias equations nonetheless remains justified, because it yields an estimate based only on studies whose reported statistics are internally consistent.

The publication-bias diagnostics were similarly nuanced. Egger's test was significant, but trim-and-fill identified no missing studies and the asymmetry disappeared when four high-leverage equations were removed. Egger's test is known to perform poorly under very high heterogeneity, and the pattern here points to a small number of studies with unusual coefficients rather than to systematic non-publication of small studies.

Equations whose coefficient deviated further from the pooled estimate also tended to report a poorer within-study fit, an association that was considerably stronger among high-risk-of-bias equations (r = `r f3(o$offset_high_r)`) than among the rest (r = `r f3(o$offset_low_r)`) despite similar mean offsets. Because the analysis-domain rating was based on internal consistency, this suggests that data-quality or reporting problems tend to show up jointly as an unusual coefficient and a poorly fitting model, rather than as independent sources of variation.

These findings can be set against earlier attempts to establish a population-independent coefficient, none of which used a meta-analytic framework. Feldesman and colleagues [@feldesman1990; @feldesman1996] and Sjøvold [@sjovold1990] pooled primary skeletal or living-sample data or averaged a simple ratio across samples, and Albanese and colleagues [@albanese2016] fitted equations to skeletal collections; none reported an I² statistic, a formal moderator test or an assessment of publication bias. The present results allow a more precise statement than the earlier conclusion that race- and sex-specific methods offer negligible improvement: country-level variation is real and statistically detectable but modest (about `r f0(o$country_primary_R2)`% of between-study variance), a middle position between a strict global constant and a fully population-specific parameter.

Numerically, the pooled coefficient can be compared with published tibia and femur coefficients, bearing in mind that percutaneous, dry-bone and radiographic lengths differ. Trotter and Gleser's dry-bone equations for American White males gave femoral slopes of 2.38 (1952) and 2.32 (1958) and, for females, 2.47 (1952) [@trotter1952; @trotter1958]; a later revision gave a tibial slope of 2.52 [@trotter1970]. In a large radiographic sample of Austrian adults (n = 4200), Simon and colleagues [@simon2023] reported tibial slopes of 2.415 (males) and 2.301 (females). Albanese and colleagues' [@albanese2016] dry-bone tibial equations gave a slope of 2.44 in their sex-specific equations and 2.89 in their generic equation. The pooled coefficient obtained here (`r f3(o$primary_b)`) lies somewhat below this range of about 2.3 to 2.9, although the male pooled coefficient (`r f3(o$primary_male_b)`) approaches its lower end. This is consistent with regression dilution: percutaneous measurement includes variable soft-tissue thickness over the condyle and malleolus and is subject to greater measurement error than dry-bone or radiographic measurement, a concern raised specifically for tibial measurement protocols [@jantz1995], and error in the predictor attenuates the estimated slope. It may also reflect the more geographically diverse populations pooled here compared with the predominantly European-ancestry samples behind the historical equations. Measurement modality is therefore a plausible contributor to the heterogeneity documented here, distinct from, and potentially confounded with, the country effect.

## Limitations

Limitations of the evidence: none of the published equations had been externally validated, and most reported no validation of any kind; the primary analysis excluded a substantial minority of the literature (`r n_high_pooled` of `r o$allstudies_k` equations) on the basis of internal consistency; these equations are not a random subset, and their exclusion shifts the pooled estimate upward relative to the full sample. The geographic distribution of the literature is uneven, with Indian studies contributing `r o$full_india` of `r o$allstudies_k` equations and several regions represented by one to four equations, which limits the precision of country- and continent-level estimates. Country is only an approximate proxy for population or ethnic group. Most samples were students or young adults, and several included 17-year-olds, although excluding those samples did not change the result. The near-total heterogeneity means that the pooled coefficient should not be applied uncritically to any particular population.

Limitations of the review process: the search was restricted to three databases and to published reports in English, `r pv["not_retrieved"]` potentially relevant reports could not be retrieved in full text (most of them from subscription-only regional journals or theses), and the review protocol was not registered in advance. The adapted PROBAST and the internal-consistency checks used in the analysis domain have not been validated for single-predictor stature equations. Finally, because only aggregate study-level data were available, the review could not determine whether population differences act through the slope or through the intercept.

# Practical application: a global slope with population-specific intercepts

The meta-regression pooled only the regression coefficient (slope); it did not, and was not designed to, estimate a pooled intercept, because pooling raw intercepts across populations with different mean stature and mean tibial length would amount to extrapolating to a tibial length of zero for a population that does not exist. The pooled slope is therefore not a complete prediction equation: an intercept appropriate to the target population must always be supplied. Combining a common slope with a population-specific intercept has precedent in this literature. Jantz [@jantz1992], revising Trotter and Gleser's female formulae, observed that the regression coefficient varies comparatively little among populations and proposed retaining the original coefficient while calculating a new intercept from the target sample's own mean stature and mean bone length. This is an instance of what the prediction-model literature calls recalibration-in-the-large [@riley2016]: holding the slope fixed and re-estimating only the intercept, which is far more data-efficient than deriving a new equation.

Three implementations are available, in increasing order of the data they require. First, mean-based recalibration needs only the target population's mean stature and mean tibial length: local intercept = mean(local stature) − b~global~ × mean(local tibial length), using the pooled coefficient (`r f3(o$primary_b)`, or `r f3(o$primary_male_b)` for males and `r f3(o$primary_female_b)` for females when sex is known). Second, where a local calibration sample with paired measurements is available, local stature can be regressed on the fixed global predictor (b~global~ × tibial length entered as an offset) so that only the intercept is estimated, which also yields a confidence interval for the local intercept. Third, with data from several populations, a mixed-effects or ANCOVA-type model can be fitted with population affecting the intercept only and a common slope.

One caveat should be explicit. The meta-regression tested whether the slopes reported by different studies differ by country; it did not show that population differences in predicted stature operate only through the intercept. Each study contributes a single fitted equation rather than individual-level data, so slope heterogeneity within populations could not be examined directly. The common-slope, population-specific-intercept approach is therefore a practical simplification supported by the narrow confidence interval of the pooled slope and by precedent [@jantz1992], not something this review proved. Where sufficient local paired data exist, testing for slope heterogeneity (for example, with a population-by-tibial-length interaction) before adopting a common slope remains the more rigorous option.

The validation status of the existing equations bears directly on when the global coefficient should be preferred. Because no published equation has been externally validated and most report no validation at all, the advantage of a local equation rests on the untested assumption that its single-sample slope transfers to new individuals, even within its own population. Where no local equation exists, where the remains may come from a different or unknown population, or where the only local equation is unvalidated, based on a small sample or at high risk of bias in the analysis domain, the global coefficient combined with a population-specific intercept is the more defensible choice. Where an internally validated local equation at low risk of bias exists for the same population, it is reasonable to retain it and to use the global coefficient as a cross-check; an externally validated local equation, once available, should take precedence for its own population. A well-conducted local equation is not necessarily inferior for its own population, because between-study heterogeneity was large relative to the sampling error of most individual slopes; whether that heterogeneity reflects true population differences or methodological variation is what external validation must establish.

# Future directions: external validation

The pooled coefficient is, in effect, a model developed from aggregate published data, and it requires external validation in independent data before it can be applied with confidence outside the populations represented here. Two questions are of particular interest: whether a slope estimated in new data is consistent with the pooled estimate, and whether the pooled slope, combined with a locally recalibrated intercept, achieves acceptable calibration and accuracy in a population not included in this synthesis. A rigorous design would recruit adults from populations under-represented in the present review using a standardized percutaneous protocol with a documented reliability assessment, and would assess calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, R², SEE and Bland–Altman limits of agreement. A multi-site design with individual-level data would also allow a mixed-effects test of whether the country-level variation detected here operates mainly through the intercept or the slope.

# Conclusion

This systematic review and meta-regression of `r pv["after_fulltext"]` studies (`r o$rob_n` equations) found a precisely estimated pooled coefficient of `r f3(o$primary_b)` (95% CI `r ci(o$primary_lb, o$primary_ub)`) for predicting stature from percutaneous tibial length, consistent with the full-sample estimate of `r f3(o$allstudies_b)` and robust to restriction by risk of bias and age. Country was a significant but modest moderator, continental grouping was not, and male and female coefficients did not differ. The coefficient is best characterized as a robust global central tendency of about 2.0 to 2.2 with modest population-specific structure and substantial unexplained heterogeneity. For forensic practice, a global coefficient combined with a population-specific intercept is a reasonable default where no validated local equation is available, which is currently the case for most populations because none of the published equations has been externally validated; internally validated local equations at low risk of bias remain reasonable choices for their own populations. Future primary studies would benefit from more geographically balanced sampling, standardized landmark definitions and routine internal-consistency checks of reported regression statistics.
